steps.label: Do Now: Data Types (Exam Question)
steps.content:
Do Now: Data Types

Think → Pair → ShareHow can you tell a value's data type just by looking at it? Try it with "Mia".Show the answer

Look at what is in the value. "Mia" has quote marks and letters: it is text, so it is a String.

items.prompt:
From 2.1. Cambridge IGCSE 0478/21, June 2024, Question 3.
State what is meant by the data types integer and real. Give an example of each.
items.context: State what is meant by the data types integer and real. Give an example of each.
scheme: Integer: a whole number / a number with no fractional part
A correct example of an integer, such as 27
Real: a number that contains a fractional part / a decimal point
A correct example of a real, such as 18.75
items.guidance: One mark for a correct statement about each data type (points 1 and 3). One mark for a correct example of data for each data type (points 2 and 4). Mark scheme example answer: Integer: a whole number [1], Example 27 [1]. Real: a number that contains a fractional part [1], Example 18.75 [1]. Each mark is independent. Accept int for integer and float for real. Simple, plain wording is fine.
items.modelAnswer: Integer: a whole number, such as 27. Real: a number with a decimal point, such as 18.75.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: what a data type means

steps.text: A similar question: state what is meant by the data type String. Give an example.
First, think of some values that have this data type.
Ask: what do all these values have in common? They are text, in quote marks.
steps.visual:
pet = "Rex"
city = "Bangkok"
code = "B12"
They are all text

steps.text: Write what it means in a few words.
steps.visual: String: text: letters, digits or symbols

steps.text: Then give one value of that data type as the example.
Now do the same for integer, then for real: think of values, find what they share, then give one example.
steps.visual: Two marks each: what it means, then an example.

half = coins - 1

steps.label: 2.2: Input and Output
steps.content:
Text-based Programming

2.2: Input and Output

Year 7

  • Today: write programs that ask the user, and show an answer.
  • The big question: why can the number a user types not be added up straight away?
Think → Pair → ShareA quiz app asks your name and then says hello to you. How does the program know your name? Why can it not know it before you type?Show the answer

You type it, and the program stores it. It only knows what you give it. Today we learn how.

steps.label: Explain It: Quote Marks or Not
steps.content:
Explain It: Quote Marks or Not

Think → Pair → ShareWhere have you seen a program show your own name on the screen?Show the answer

A game shows your player name. A website says Welcome and your name. Each user sees a different name.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: The animation ran name = "Mia", print("Hi"), print(name) and print("name"). Line 1 stored "Mia" in the variable name. print("Hi") showed Hi, without the quote marks. print(name) has no quote marks, so Python looked in the variable and showed Mia. print("name") showed the word name. In your own words, explain why print(name) shows Mia, but print("name") shows name.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why print(name) shows Mia, but print("name") shows name.
scheme: Without quote marks, name is a variable, so print shows the value it holds (Mia)
With quote marks, "name" is text / a String, so print shows it exactly as written
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "It has quote marks" alone earns nothing.
items.modelAnswer: name is a variable, so print shows what it holds: Mia. "name" in quote marks is text, so it is shown as written.

steps.label: Explain It: What input Gives
steps.content:
Explain It: What input Gives

Think → Pair → ShareA user types their phone number into a program. Will the program ever add 1 to it? Why?Show the answer

No. A phone number is a label, not an amount. Nobody does maths with it.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: The animation ran age = input("Age? ") and print(age). input() showed the question Age? on the screen and waited. The user typed 12 and pressed Enter. What was typed went into the variable age as the String "12": input() always gives a String, even when the user types digits. print(age) showed 12. The user types 12 into age = input("Age? "). In your own words, explain what data type age holds, and why.
items.prompt: The user types 12 into age = input("Age? "). In your own words, explain what data type age holds, and why.
scheme: age holds a String / text, not a number
input() always gives a String / text, even for digits
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "It holds 12" alone earns nothing.
items.modelAnswer: A String. input() always gives a String, even when the user types digits.

steps.label: Explain It: Why int()?
steps.content:
Explain It: Why int()?

Think → Pair → ShareWhere else must you change something into a different form before you can use it?Show the answer

Money into a different currency before you spend it abroad. Frozen food thawed before you cook it.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: The animation ran print("3" + 1): "3" is a String and 1 is an Integer, and the program stopped with an error. Then int() turned the String "3" into the Integer 3, so print(int("3") + 1) showed 4. float("2.5") gave the Real 2.5; int("2.5") stopped with an error; str(12) gave the String "12". In your own words, explain why print("3" + 1) stops with an error, but print(int("3") + 1) shows 4.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why print("3" + 1) stops with an error, but print(int("3") + 1) shows 4.
scheme: "3" is a String / text, and + cannot add a String and a number
int() turns "3" into the Integer / number 3, so + adds 3 + 1
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "It is wrong" earns nothing.
items.modelAnswer: "3" is a String, so + cannot add 1 to it. int() makes it the number 3, so 3 + 1 = 4.

steps.label: Compare: age + 1
steps.content:
Compare: age + 1

Think → Pair → ShareBoth programs do age + 1. How can one of them work and not the other?Show the answer

Talk in pairs about the data type of age in each program. Then choose your answer.

The user types 12 into each program.

Program A

age = input("Age? ")
print(age + 1)

Program B

age = int(input("Age? "))
print(age + 1)

items.prompt: What happens in each program, and why?
options: A stops with an error and B prints 13: A adds 1 to a String
A prints 121 and B prints 13: A joins the 1 to the 12
A prints 13 and B prints 13: Python can see the digits
A prints 13 and B stops with an error: int() cannot read 12
items.explain: In A, age is the String "12". Python cannot add the number 1 to a String, so it stops with an error. In B, int() makes age the Integer 12, so age + 1 is 13.

steps.label: Explain It: Why str()?
steps.content:
Explain It: Why str()?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do programs show words next to a number, like "Score: 7"?Show the answer

The words tell the user what the number means. 7 alone could mean anything.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: The animation ran age = 12 and print("Age: " + age): + was given the String "Age: " and the Integer 12, and the program stopped with an error. Then str(age) turned 12 into the String "12", so + joined two Strings and showed Age: 12. A comma, print("Age:", age), also showed Age: 12. age holds 12. In your own words, explain why print("Age: " + age) stops with an error, and how str() fixes it.
items.prompt: age holds 12. In your own words, explain why print("Age: " + age) stops with an error, and how str() fixes it.
scheme: + cannot join a String and an Integer / a number
str() turns 12 into the String "12", so + joins two Strings
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "Use str()" alone earns nothing: it must make the number text.
items.modelAnswer: + cannot join text and a number. str(age) makes 12 the String "12", so + joins them.

steps.label: Explain: Why 34?
steps.content:
Explain: Why 34?

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

Two connected points: why it goes wrong, and what fixes it, joined with "so" or "because".

A program has a = input(), b = input() and print(a + b). The user types 3 and 4. It prints 34.

items.prompt: Explain why it prints 34, and how to make it print 7.
items.context: A Python program has a = input(), b = input() and print(a + b). The user types 3 and 4. It prints 34. Explain why it prints 34, and how to make it print 7.
scheme: input() gives a String / text, so + joins "3" and "4"
Use int() round input() / int(input()), so a and b are Integers and + adds them
items.guidance: Award 1 mark for each point. Accept "they are text" for String. Accept float() for the fix. Do not accept "it is wrong" or "use numbers" alone.
items.modelAnswer: input() gives a String, so + joins "3" and "4" (1 mark). Use int(input()) so a and b are Integers, and + adds them (1 mark).
